source.title: Progressive Residual Warmup for Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Tian-Long Chen; Xin Xu; Lu Yin; Hao Chen; Yang Wang; Shi-Zhe Diao; Can Yang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equation and appendix figure text is garbled, but the main results tables and prose are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a residual-training intervention in decoder-only language models and reports perplexity and stability results, extending the training-optimization topic to a different model family, task, and measure.
record.gate_note: The study reports language-model perplexity and stability, not training classification error on CIFAR or the other behaviors named by V1–V6. The paper cites prior findings about layerwise convergence and normalization but does not test those cited results directly.
record.test_reason: The study uses residual connections and normalization in a new Transformer training method and evaluates that method's performance. It does not test any V1–V6 outcome: its depth comparisons retain residual connections, its initialization comparisons use residual Transformers, and its stability analyses do not measure learning-rate stability thresholds or curvature.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: progressive residual scheduling improves Transformer pretraining performance and stability. Qualify its depth-scaling statement: the depth sweep applies ProRes only to Pre-LN, whereas the main fixed-depth experiments cover multiple initialization and normalization schemes. Schedule ablations also show that some alternative schedules degrade performance or diverge.
record.recipe_differences: Uses AdamW to pretrain decoder-only language models and modifies residual branches with a progressive scaling schedule; it does not use the classification-training recipes or datasets in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with architecture, ProRes schedule and warmup length, model scale, and initialization/normalization variant. The linear schedule works broadly; equal and reverse schedules can degrade performance or diverge in some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: ProRes reduces held-out C4-en perplexity in all 21 Table 2 comparisons. Improvements range from 0.04 to 1.09 perplexity points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressive residual warmup can improve held-out language-model perplexity across the tested residual Transformer architectures, initialization schemes, and model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.4 reports better depth scaling and near-zero loss-spike scores with ProRes in Pre-LN Transformers through 120 layers. All compared architectures retain residual connections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressive residual warmup can improve depth scaling and reduce training spikes in residual Pre-LN Transformers.

record.problems: The reported main tables give test perplexity, not training classification error. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these comparisons. The text describes depth-scaling and stability figures, but does not provide their underlying numeric values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reasoning benchmark accuracy, Table 4 WikiText/LAMBADA perplexity, Table 6 schedule-ablation perplexity, ClimbMix Table 7, and figure-only depth and spike results are omitted because the claim versions concern training classification error or other specifically named training behaviors; the study's results do not measure those version outcomes.

untested.parts: Training classification error in large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random or corrupted labels and recipe-dependent failures.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks and their reduction through extra student neurons.
Depth-related training-error degradation in plain convolutional networks versus identity-shortcut networks; very deep plain tanh initialization and normalization-free Fixup training.

Activation-matched initialization controlling signal and gradient propagation to improve speed and trainable depth in plain networks; Gaussian versus orthogonal weights and orthogonal convolution kernels.
Loss recovery above the initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to a measured stability threshold.
Batch normalization versus no batch normalization for accuracy gain speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup's normalization-free residual training comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The T3 assignment is unsupported because a new setting must still measure a named version's effect. All recorded numerical pairs match Table 2, but they are comparisons of the proposed method's performance. Their observed/partial states should not be interpreted as evidence about V1–V6. The omitted depth, spike, schedule, and 7B loss results likewise do not establish those versions.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, optimizer, early stopping, and regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus identity-shortcut convolutional networks and training classification error; no CIFAR or ImageNet classification training-error comparison.
Activation-matched initialization, signal or gradient propagation, Gaussian versus orthogonal initialization, and trainable depth in plain networks.
Learning rates above a stability limit, curvature or sharpness thresholds, and loss recovery or divergence in the stated squared-loss settings.
Batch normalization's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance in the stated vision settings, and Fixup comparisons.
